Triggers.value: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel like I don't know myself anymore
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
I can't rely on other people

issues.item: Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: 'Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of natural disaster. A car-crash-specific trigger suggests a different index trauma unless there is clear disaster-related context, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
issues.explanation: 'Rage on Recall' is not well supported by the rest of the profile, which otherwise centers on fear, vulnerability, dissociation/gaps, and interpersonal mistrust after a natural disaster. Intense rage could occur clinically, but here it lacks corroboration from threat or appraisal items and weakens overall coherence.

For a natural disaster trauma, 'related people' as a primary trigger is hard to justify unless they were directly linked to the event; with no supporting interpersonal trauma content elsewhere, this trigger is clinically questionable.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
issues.explanation: The threat item about unusual silence implying imminent danger fits combat/interpersonal danger contexts more than natural disaster exposure, and it is not supported by the trigger or appraisal content here.

vignette:
# Marcus

Marcus was twenty-six when the hurricane hit. He had been working as a junior salesman for a commercial real estate firm in Charleston, South Carolina, living alone in a modest apartment two blocks from the harbor. He was ambitious, well-liked by colleagues, the kind of person who made plans and followed through on them. When Hurricane Ophelia made landfall that September, Marcus had stayed behind to help a coworker secure the office building—a decision that seemed practical at the time, even noble. What he had not anticipated was the violence of the surge, the way the water rose not gradually but in a sudden, suffocating wall that trapped him in the stairwell between the first and second floors. He remembered the cold shock of it, the absolute darkness, the sound of concrete cracking. After that, the memory fractured. He knew he had made it to the roof, that he had been rescued by helicopter at dawn, but the hours in between existed only as a sensation—a crushing weight, a roaring in his ears, a terror so absolute it had no shape or image to contain it. When he tried later to piece together what had happened, whole sections simply would not come back to him, no matter how hard he concentrated. The gaps themselves became another kind of dread.

Three years later, Marcus still could not make sense of who he had become in the aftermath. The man who had weathered the hurricane was not the same person who now sat in his car in parking lots, checking his phone compulsively, unable to go inside. He had come to believe that he could not trust his own judgment anymore—if he had misjudged the storm's severity once, how could he trust himself about anything? This conviction had spread into every corner of his thinking. He could not rely on other people, either; the coworker he had tried to help had moved away without staying in touch, and Marcus had interpreted this as confirmation that his presence was a burden, that people ultimately could not be counted on. Nothing felt meaningful anymore. His job, which had once excited him, now felt hollow—he would sit across from clients and pitch commercial properties while some part of him remained trapped in that stairwell, and the disconnect was so profound that he had stopped believing his own words. He was no longer sure what he wanted or who he was trying to be.

Certain moments would crack open this fragile equilibrium. When a client asked him to meet at a waterfront restaurant to discuss a development project, Marcus felt the old terror surge through his body before any conscious thought could intervene. The vulnerability of being near water, of being in a space where he could not control the environment, would trigger a cascade of intrusive memories—not clear images, but the raw emotional intensity of drowning, of helplessness, of the moment when he had been certain he would die. These moments of feeling emotionally vulnerable would send him spiraling into the memory itself, and the memory would confirm his darkest beliefs: that he was fundamentally unsafe, that he could not trust his own mind, that the world was far more dangerous than he had ever understood. When he forced himself to attend his company's quarterly meeting at a hotel with a view of the harbor, the sight of open water triggered the same cycle. His heart would race, his palms would sweat, and suddenly he was back in that darkness, feeling the full terror of the event as if it were happening in real time. He would excuse himself and sit in his car for an hour, unable to return.

The hypervigilance had become constant. Marcus woke most nights at three or four in the morning, his body already alert, checking his phone, checking the weather, checking that his apartment door was locked. He had begun to avoid anything that resembled the conditions of the disaster—he would not go to the beach, would not hike near rivers, would not even sit outside during heavy rain. But the avoidance itself had become a kind of prison. He had turned down a promotion that would have required occasional travel to coastal cities. He had stopped seeing friends who suggested outdoor activities. The isolation only deepened his sense that he was fundamentally alone, that no one could understand what he had lost or who he had become. His negative appraisals—the conviction that he was broken, that nothing mattered, that other people could not be trusted—seemed to generate their own evidence. Each time he declined an invitation, each time he failed to show up for a social commitment because the anxiety felt unbearable, he saw it as proof of his own inadequacy. And each proof seemed to trigger the memories again, the fragmentary, terrifying sensations that had no clear beginning or end.

It was his mother who finally insisted he seek help. She had noticed his weight loss, his increasing isolation, the way he would freeze when it rained. Marcus had resisted for months, but last week he had woken from a nightmare so vivid—not a memory, exactly, but the emotion of drowning without any image to anchor it—that he had sat on his bed until dawn, unable to move. He called a therapist that morning. What he wanted most was to feel like himself again, to believe that the world was not fundamentally hostile, to trust that other people—and his own mind—might not betray him. He was not sure such a thing was possible anymore, but he had finally become desperate enough to try.
